reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
clinicalPearls: Follows head trauma, often a temporal-bone or occipital impact, without a visible fracture of the otic capsule
Presents with sensorineural hearing loss, frequently in the higher frequencies, together with tinnitus and vertigo or imbalance beginning soon after the injury
Vertigo may be constant at first and then settle, or may present as positional vertigo if otoconia are dislodged (traumatic BPPV)
The mechanism is an energy or pressure wave transmitted through the skull to the membranous labyrinth and hair cells, causing microscopic damage without frank bony disruption
It is a diagnosis of exclusion - temporal-bone fracture, perilymph fistula, ossicular disruption, and central brain injury must be ruled out
Management is largely supportive, with vestibular rehabilitation for persistent imbalance and repositioning manoeuvres for traumatic BPPV, while hearing loss is often permanent
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone and audiometry are central to distinguishing it from fracture and conductive causes
reference.pathophysiology: A blow to the head transmits kinetic energy through the skull to the fluid-filled inner ear even when the bony otic capsule stays intact. The resulting pressure wave and shearing forces damage the delicate cochlear and vestibular hair cells and their supporting structures, and may dislodge utricular otoconia into the semicircular canals. Cochlear injury produces sensorineural hearing loss, classically affecting higher frequencies, together with tinnitus, while vestibular injury causes vertigo and disequilibrium. Because the damage is at the cellular level rather than a gross fracture, imaging is frequently normal, and the diagnosis rests on the temporal relationship to trauma and on exclusion of other injuries.
additionalDifferentials: Temporal bone fracture, otic-capsule sparing or violating
Ossicular chain disruption causing conductive loss
Post-concussion syndrome or central vestibular injury
Acoustic trauma from an associated blast
additionalInvestigations: Pure-tone audiometry to document the pattern and degree of hearing loss
High-resolution CT of the temporal bone to exclude fracture
Tympanometry to assess middle-ear and ossicular status
MRI of the brain if central injury is suspected
redFlags: Progressive or fluctuating hearing loss suggesting a perilymph fistula
Otorrhoea or clear fluid leak raising concern for a CSF fistula
Focal neurological deficit or deteriorating conscious level
Vertigo accompanied by severe or worsening headache
reference.prognosis: Vertigo and imbalance often improve over weeks to months through central compensation and vestibular rehabilitation, but sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus are frequently permanent.
pitfalls: Attributing all post-traumatic dizziness to concussion and missing a perilymph fistula or temporal-bone fracture
Overlooking traumatic BPPV, which is readily treated with repositioning manoeuvres
Failing to obtain baseline audiometry, which is important both clinically and medicolegally after head injury
Missing a co-existing CSF leak or facial nerve injury
references: Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Manage supportively as there is no specific pharmacological cure, using vestibular suppressants such as prochlorperazine or an antihistamine only briefly for severe acute vertigo to avoid delaying central compensation
Refer for vestibular rehabilitation exercises to promote central compensation for persistent imbalance
Perform canalith repositioning manoeuvres such as the Epley if traumatic benign paroxysmal positional vertigo develops from dislodged otoconia
Provide audiological rehabilitation with hearing aids for persistent sensorineural hearing loss and offer tinnitus management strategies
Exclude and treat associated injuries such as temporal-bone fracture, perilymph fistula, ossicular disruption or central brain injury
Give falls-prevention and safety advice during the recovery period
Coordinate ENT, audiology and vestibular therapy follow-up to monitor recovery
